draft.title: Financial trends
card: A financial trend is the way a money figure changes over time, such as prices, interest rates, wages or house prices. Looking at data over several years shows the pattern, not just one number.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks the price of a typical basket of goods and services. If the CPI rises from 100 to 105, prices have risen by 5%.
Wages show what people earn. If prices rise by 5% and wages rise by 2%, a worker can buy less than before, even though their pay went up.
Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Example: a wage rises from $1000 to $1030 a week. The change is 30 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 3%.
draft.remember: Compare how fast prices and wages change: if prices rise faster than wages, buying power falls.

a.q: The CPI rises from 120 to 126 over a year. By what percentage have prices risen?
a.why: The change is 126 − 120 = 6. Then 6 ÷ 120 × 100 = 5%. Using 6 as the percentage forgets to divide by the old value, which is the tempting mistake.
a.clue: Divide the change by the starting value.

b.q: Over a year, Sam's wage rises by 2% and prices rise by 4%. What has happened to what Sam's wage can buy?
opts: It has fallen, as prices rose faster than the wage
It has risen, as the wage went up by 2%
It has stayed the same, as both figures rose
It has fallen, as the wage rose by less than 4 dollars
b.why: Prices rose by more than the wage, so each dollar buys less and Sam can afford less than before. A pay rise alone does not mean buying power rises, because it must be compared with price changes.
b.clue: Compare the two percentages, not just the wage.

b.best: It has fallen, as prices rose faster than the wage

check.summary: No problems found. The card's CPI, wage and percentage-change facts are correct, and both questions have one clear right answer that matches the explanations.
